Let the darkness of Amelia give you welcome.

Brutal, But Just (Part 3/Finale)
An Amelia City Story
By Joshua T. Calkins-Treworgy

#fiction
#horror
#WritingCommunity

Part III- Decisions

“Hell is empty, and all the devils are here.”
-William Shakespeare

     “Well, shit,” Julio muttered to himself, hanging up on the attempted call. The number on the back of the private investigator’s card had gone to a dead end, an automated voice informing him that the number he was trying to dial was out of service. He followed this up by quickly hopping on the computer at his desk in the bullpen, and performing a quick search through the state of Iowa’s register for licensed private investigators. When no match for the name ‘Roderick Stranger’ came up, he felt a tightening in his gut, and thought, Oh, I fucked up. Immediately he sped down into the basement level of the station, bursting into Quinn’s fortress and startling the pale young computer tech enough to cause her to nearly fall back in her wheeled chair. Pinwheeling her arms, she barely maintained herself in an upright position, and she panted for a moment, glaring up at him. 
     “Where’s the fire there, big guy,” she squeaked. 
     “I need you to pull up and look through the last couple of hours of interior footage from the station, first and third floors, and the steps coming inside,” Julio said curtly. He handed her the P.I.’s card. “This guy came by, claiming he was looking into Biker on behalf of a private client, but the number’s disconnected, and his name doesn’t come up in the PI registration for the state. We have facial recognition software, though, right?”
     “Some of the newest and most expensive,” Quinn replied with a wry grin. “Let me take a look see here,” she said, wheeling herself over to a different workstation from the one she had been at when he burst in. Using her keyboard and maneuvering at her uncanny speed, she brought up the footage from the station’s main entrance steps and did a quick jump back to around the time the man calling himself Roderick would have arrived. Julio leaned down over her shoulder to look at the screen, and the same sense of ‘unreality’ that had afflicted him in the PI’s presence settled in the back of his mind as the man stepped into frame-
     and the area of the screen from the man’s shoulders up to the top of his wide-brimmed travelers’ hat instantly distorted, creating a kind of blurred out effect on the display. The distortion didn’t affect the entire screen from one side to the other, like some kind of digital artifact, no; it only appeared to affect Roderick’s head and shoulders, and for some reason, his hat. Quinn shook her head quickly, switching to the feed from the front duty desk, but here, she and Julio found the effect held steady, continuing to blur out the man’s countenance. She let out a shaky breath and eased back in her chair, and Julio, feeling a shudder pass through him, stepped back.
     “What the fuck is this,” he finally asked after a minute’s silence. 
     “It’s Amelia,” Quinn answered, exiting out of the station video archives program. “And I hope that it has nothing to do with us.”
**
     Two days later, and one more victim had been claimed by the MAP Hunter. Jacob Coggins, a high school chemistry teacher, had been found in his classroom after hours, the school’s fire alarm system having been activated and bringing the fire department. Shortly after firefighters had arrived, however, they ended up putting in a call to the ACPD’s Homicide Division, which drew Julio and a few other detectives.
     At first, it seemed like it might have been a student revenge kind of thing, as the teacher had been, according to the M.E., set on fire with one of his own Bunsen burners, after his head had been rammed down onto it, the device shoved into his eye socket before being activated. But Julio spotted the chalkboard, and the other two detectives from his division who had responded left it to him when they saw it as well; the claw insignia that had been at all of his previous victim’s locations had been scrawled in chalk upon it. Combined with a set of Polaroids found splayed out on the man’s desk left no room for confusion- this victim had been another pedophile. 
     Upon returning to his home station, Julio was immediately summoned into the Captain’s office, where the Commissioner stood waiting like a gargoyle in the corner of the room. The man had all the charm and physicality of a drowned sewer rat, and when he began snarling at the detective, Julio’s already low opinion of the man didn’t improve. “Detective, I’m starting to wonder if you maybe forgot what your job here is,” the Commissioner began, slowly creeping out from his corner like a snake on two legs, his movements oily, his entire body above the waist barely moving. “We have a killer at large in my city now, and the papers and the fucking blogs have all decided to even give him a cute little nickname!” These last three words came out in a snapping shout as the man came to a stop just a couple of feet away from Julio, his brow furrowed, forehead shiny with a cold sweat. 
     “I’ve heard, sir,” Julio replied evenly. “They’re calling him ‘The MAP Hunter’, sir.”
     “I know! A moniker that, apparently, one of our own people was overheard saying a couple of victims ago when they were leaving the scene with the body; he couldn’t have known that there was a local crime blogger listening in. But worse for you, detective Ramos, is that I have personally been digging around among your colleagues, and I know that it was you who started using that term,” the Commissioner growled, jabbing a crooked finger a hair’s breadth from Julio’s chest. “I know you’re not exactly fond of these men who are getting killed; not many people are. But they are citizens of our city, and they deserve justice, just the same as anybody else.”
     Julio summoned all of his willpower to avoid saying, Maybe they already got their justice, sir. It was not an easy effort to keep his mouth shut. “Quinn and I are trying to find any kind of deeper common tie between all of these guys, sir, but so far, we keep hitting dead ends,” Julio said. 
     “Well, you had better find your man, detective,” the Commissioner said, stomping toward the office door. The Captain, Julio noted, had been sitting silently in his seat across his desk, scowling at the Commissioner’s back the whole time. “You’re not being paid to just let these things happen.” When the man was gone, Julio turned to Captain Tillert and snorted. 
     “He’s a little hot under the collar about this,” Julio commented. 
     “Yes, he is. But unfortunately, I sort of get it. This city has enough weirdness and shadows to contend with on a regular daily basis, and adding a serial killer on top just makes it all the worse. You remember that City Councilwoman who was found cuffed to a street lamp earlier this year? Beaten and ripped apart with a claw hammer?”
     “Shit, yeah, I remember that,” Julio said with a heavy sigh. “Lot of people got killed around the city that night, and some of those were really weird,” he added, tilting his head slightly to one side. “What’s that got to do with this?” The Captain reached into one of his desk drawers, pulling out a plain manila folder and setting it on his desk, sliding it toward Julio, who opened it up. 
     “Take a look at the graffiti on that precinct house wall, detective,” Tillert said. “Tell me what you notice.” It took Julio all of five seconds to spot it; the claw insignia, once more showing up in all of its occult glory. He closed the folder and slid it back. “I didn’t show that to the Commissioner, but I’m showing it to you for one reason.”
     “Why’s that, sir?”
     “Because it seems like, more often than not, when this symbol pops up near a crime scene, we never end up getting any straight answers.” Julio gave his superior a wordless nod and headed out of the office, thinking that this wasn’t always going to be the case, because he had seen that claw symbol one other place, and recently. It hadn’t stuck with him right away, and thinking on it now, he could kick himself for not having called notice to it the moment he had seen it.
     It had been on the knife sheath of Roderick Stranger, Private Investigator.

**

     “The sonofabitch was in arm’s reach,” Julio grumbled a few hours later, as he and a team of crime scene techs observed what remained of Assan Biker. “He was right in front of me, and I let him go.” The M.E. and his assistant wordlessly motioned Julio to back away from the mutilated remains, rolling the body over. The assistant let out a groan as they did so, and quickly shuffled away after helping put the body bag under the victim. “What’s with Jerry? He’s not usually squeamish,” Julio observed to the M.E.
     “He likely just spotted what I did, detective,” the older man replied with a grimace. “Your victim’s severed, ah, ‘appendage’, is accounted for. It appears to have been shoved up his backside.” Julio sucked air through clenched teeth, shaking his head. The savagery that had gone into this latest attack had been swift, however, and much sloppier than the previous victims, likely as a result of the MAP Hunter (Julio hated himself for mentally accepting this label, but there it was) having felt the heat of the closing circle of law enforcement. The detective waved the M.E. off, then headed back through the luxury condo for Biker’s bedroom.
     Much to his surprise, none of the scene techs had been in the room yet, from all appearances. Julio cast a quick glance around the room, spotting an open laptop sitting on the bed. He made his way around with his latex gloves to retrieve it, halting as he spotted something resting on the dead man’s pillow- a small business card.
     For one Roderick Stranger, PI.
     On the back was written the following: “Come alone, detective.” Following this was an address, one he knew only vaguely from when he had first moved to the area of Amelia City. Between Amelia proper and North Perry, off the long, quiet country road that connected the city itself with its largest suburb, there was an old Iowa Highway Patrol station that had been out of service for a long time. He’d been out there twice since arriving in Amelia City, each time tracking rumors and street hubbub that resulted in the discovery of people who had gone missing and were presumed dead. 
     Julio pocketed the card in his front pants pocket, closed the laptop, and brought it out into the living room, handing it over to a scene tech before excusing himself from the condo.  

**

     Sometimes, when a person is confronted with the bizarre or the absurd, their brain performs a kind of trick in order to protect itself, shutting out entirely certain personal sensory input, then slowly allowing it to filter through to the conscious mind. Over the course of history, people who experience this phenomenon have frequently described the sensation as a kind of tingling or itching that creeps over their scalp. Detective Julio Ramos underwent this sensation as he idled his unmarked cruiser along the gravel pathway that led off the county road and through a wooded thicket toward the abandoned Highway Patrol station. 
     The first of the oddities was the rapid onset of darkness, which only came to his tangible attention about fifty yards down the path when the vehicle’s sensor-activated headlights suddenly sprang alight to reveal the way ahead. At first, he thought nothing of it; after all, sunset was coming earlier and earlier as the season worked its way towards the first snowfalls in the region. But a quick glance over at the dashboard’s clock made this a curiosity that deserved a second glance, because according to that clock, it was only three in the afternoon. 
     The second oddity landed gently in his ears as he pulled into the natural archway between the trees which opened up into a cracked but paved parking area in front of the decrepit old Highway Patrol station. His radio, which had previously been offering a quiet but audible string of Top 40 tunes, had at some point abruptly changed to a kind of discordant jumble of classical instrumentation, strings and brass and woodwinds all seeming to play a jangled mess of mismatched tunes. It’s like a 7th grade orchestra of kids all playing off of different sheet music books, he thought, pulling the cruiser into a faded spot fronting the concrete walkway up into the building proper.  The third oddity, though it perhaps should not have surprised him, was the fact that the four tall arc sodium lamps flanking the front walkway of the station were working, dimly illuminating the area. 
     As Julio clambered up out of his vehicle, he instinctively thumbed loose the clasp button on his holster, clearing his firearm free and flipping the safety off. “Not sure you’re going to need that, boy scout,” someone said nearby in a voice that sounded like it belonged at the original Woodstock music festival. Julio shifted toward the direction of the voice, the barrel of his weapon held steady toward the ground, per his training, and immediately he felt his mouth dry up and his throat clench in preparation of a scream. Standing just off to one side of the walkway on the grass, just visible in the span of the lamplight, was what appeared to be a cow, placidly chewing a mouthful of grass. But to call it simply a cow would be rather limited, given its unique qualities; its coat did not appear to be the traditional black and white, for one thing. No, this specimen, standing in profile to Julio, head turned to look directly at him as it chewed, appeared to have a coat colored in the various hues of the rainbow, in wide but equal-sized stripes. From its underside hung an udder sack that appeared to be covered in some kind of necrotic rot, oozing a kind of sickly green pus from pustules pocking its surface. The smell of the thing, a blend of decay and, for some reason, coffee, jarred Julio’s sense of reason almost as hard as the sight of it. 
     And on its head, there stood two sets of eyes. The normal, bovine eyes just sort of looked at him with a half-lidded glare, while above them, a set of glowing, scarlet slashes glimmered balefully at him. The voice, the words, had come from the cow. “What the fuck,” Julio managed to croak.
     “I wouldn’t leave the man inside waiting too long,” the cow replied, its words carrying cleanly despite the fact that it still looked, for all intents and purposes, to be chewing its cud methodically. “He ain’t exactly the most patient guy I ever worked with.” Julio felt his gorge rising, and the urge to raise his weapon and pump multiple rounds into this bovine abomination nearly won the day. The only thing that kept his weapon down was the recognition that this, thing, was perhaps the most Amelia City thing he had ever come across. What would be the point of trying to shoot it, he mused. It’s like so much else in this godforsaken city; there, but not really there.
     Steeling himself, and with his weapon still in hand, Julio forced himself to look away from the Technicolor cow and march up the cracked walkway toward the station. The glass door fronting the station appeared to be covered in a layer of grime, obscuring his view inside until he pulled it open, revealing a front vestibule that had been turned into what looked like some kind of old-fashioned hunters’ lodge, complete with a working fireplace, a crackling fire warming the broad chamber opposite where Julio stood.
     Dominating the center of the room was what appeared to be a figure bound to an old wooden chair, largely covered under some kind of blanket. Seated just a few feet away, his long, wicked-looking blade resting on his leg, was the queer cowboy fellow himself, Roderick, his facial features no longer obscured in the light thrown from the fireplace and a nearby lamp. He was a ruggedly handsome sort, with the windburned, stubbly cheeks one might see on an Old Western gunfighter, which struck Julio as perfectly in keeping with the rest of his overall portrayal. 
     “I was starting to wonder if you were gonna show up, detective,” Roderick intoned, not turning his head to look Julio’s way, but instead still keeping his face toward the unidentified figure struggling against his rope bonds in the chair nearby. “But Clancy tells me you came alone, which is good. He can’t give milk, but he’s a good lookout when one is required.” The odd man rose from his seat, and pointed with the tip of his blade toward a small, round table off to one side of the room, to Julio’s right, where there stood an open laptop computer. “You should have a look at that, detective Ramos. It’s interesting reading.” Roderick flapped his blade toward Julio as if to prompt him into approaching the computer.
     Training took over, and Julio, responding to the blade’s movement, fired two rounds into the man’s head. Roderick’s head snapped backward, but the rest of his body didn’t move so much as an inch. Slowly, cartoonishly slowly, Roderick brought his head back down, blood streaming down his face in a thin rivulet that turned into barely a trickle as a pair of crumpled bullets pushed back out of his head, dropping to the floor. Julio watched, his throat almost clenching shut, as the gunshot wound, widened from the back-to-back shots, suctioned closed, as if nothing had happened, and the blood on Roderick’s face faded away. The knife hand swept from its tip pointing at the computer, to now pointing at the detective.
     “Put the knife down,” Julio barked in response, raising his weapon and aiming square at the side of Roderick’s head. The cowboy fellow slowly turned his head to look at Julio, his weapon arm lowering to his side at the same time. “Drop it!” 
     “Detective, I’m not in the habit of taking orders from much of anybody, except the bird,” the stranger said evenly, though with a slight hint of menace threaded through his tone, the corners of his mouth tugging down. “He runs the show around here, so I haven’t really got a choice in that; he made me what I am, and he can just as easily unmake me, I suspect. But you?” Roderick shook his head, and the frown quirked into a wry grin. “No, sir. Besides, I’m pretty sure you know exactly what would happen if you pulled that trigger on me again.” 
     Julio slipped his index finger back inside the trigger guard, cold sweat beading on the back of his neck. Yes, he did indeed understand precisely what would happen if he once more shot the creature calling itself Roderick- a bullet wound would appear, but the thing would not be stopped, and faster than he could blink, Julio Ramos would find himself choking on his own blood with that blade buried in either his throat or his chest. He slid his finger out of the trigger guard, thumbed the safety back on, and holstered the weapon. 
     “Wise choice,” Roderick rumbled, once more pointing toward the laptop with his knife. “Read.” Julio, his legs feeling like they might fold under him at any moment now, caught a whiff of the man now, a blend of tobacco, whiskey and sweat. He strode over to the table, and started scanning the screen. There appeared to be two windows open, side by side, and he moved the cursor over the left window, reading through what appeared to be several chat exchanges between someone dubbed ‘Blockerman’ and several other individuals. After a few exchanges, Julio realized that he recognized several of these usernames; they were victims of the MAP Hunter. 
     The right-hand window appeared to be an online banking account, and it showed a series of funds transfers from third parties, all of them also victims in Julio’s case. Scrolling to the top of the page, Julio felt his stomach twist as he discovered who was receiving money from the pedophiles. He whipped his head to look over at Roderick, who now stood right next to his restrained victim, his left hand holding the covering blanket. With a single twist, the cowboy-like figure tossed the blanket aside, revealing a bucking, thrashing Commissioner with a sock gag stuffed in his mouth and a swollen, blackened left eye. 
     “This man touched no innocent child himself, you see, detective,” said Roderick evenly. “But he did accept money to make sure that everybody under his command either looked in the wrong places, or went about handling ‘more important’ cases. He protected these depraved cretins, who knows for how long.” Julio shook his head slightly, unsure of himself. The evidence of what Roderick was saying was plain as day, right there on that laptop screen, but he had to wonder how much of this could be trusted as real, definitive proof. Given all of the absurdity he had witnessed since the start of this case, especially since arriving at this abandoned Highway Patrol station, how could he be sure?
     But this question was shunted aside in his mind almost immediately with another, much more reasonable one, a question he could actually ask out loud. “Why? What does any of this have to do with, you? With whatever you are,” he asked, forcing himself to sound more controlled than he felt. 
     “I wasn’t lying about everything before, you know,” Roderick replied. “I really am something of a detective myself. I find people around this city, these towns, who are just up to no good, and I just sort of, even the scales, as it were,” he said, holding up his free hand and waggling it back and forth. “That’s the task that was given to me. It’s my duty, you see. You know about duty, detective Ramos, don’t you? Isn’t that why you became a law enforcement officer?”
     “This,” Julio said, shaking his head and sniffling, on the verge of losing his failing grasp on sanity. “This isn’t the same thing.”
     “You’re quite right,” said Roderick. “It’s a close cousin, though. And much as you might want to deny it, you know as well as I do that my way, Amelia’s way, is necessary sometimes. It’s brutal, but it’s just. Now, I understand full well that you may feel the need to protect this man, to save him from me,” said Roderick, now aiming his blade at the moaning Commissioner. “You may want to place him under arrest, and present that computer of his as evidence in a case to have him locked up and sent away for the rest of his corrupt little life. I can understand that,” Roderick said with a grave nod. “I can even respect it. If you feel that’s what you have to do, I will not stop you. But you have a choice to make right now, detective. Will this man face the justice of the system sworn to by detective Julio Ramos,” he asked, pointing the tip of the blade toward Julio. “Or will he face the one sworn to by the stranger named Roderick, He of the Blade,” he continued, pointing the tip at the underside of his own stubble-heavy chin. 
     Julio looked to the computer, to the Commissioner, and then lastly, to the stranger named Roderick. He hung his head after a moment, then made several motions. He set his badge and his gun, still in its holster, on the round table, beside the laptop computer, and turned his back on the stranger and the Commissioner, letting out a long, heavy sigh. “Will they find the computer?”
     “I will make sure of it,” said Roderick behind him. “But they will not find your gun or your badge here, Julio. This I promise and swear in the name of Amelia. Now, go. Your duty here to the innocent is complete.” Julio strode away then, back out onto the station’s front walkway, back to the car. He would never again serve the people of Amelia; that, he determined, could be left to the queer mercies of the city’s otherworldly denizens.

-Fin

Beaten and ripped apart with a claw hammer?” “Shit, yeah, I remember that,” Julio said with a heavy sigh. “Lot of people got killed around the city that night, and some of those were really weird,” he added, tilting his head slightly to one side. “What’s that got to do with this?” The Captain reached into one of his desk drawers, pulling out a plain Manila folder and setting it on his desk, sliding it toward Julio, who opened it up. “Take a look at the graffiti on that precinct house wall, detective,” Tillert said. “Tell me what you notice.” It took Julio all of five seconds to spot it; the claw insignia, once more showing up in all of its occult glory. He closed the folder and slid it back. “I didn’t show that to the Commissioner, but I’m showing it to you for one reason.” “Why’s that, sir?” “Because it seems like, more often than not, when this symbol pops up near a crime scene, we never end up getting any straight answers.” Julio gave his superior a wordless nod and headed out of the office, thinking that this wasn’t always going to be the case, because he had seen that claw symbol one other place, and recently. It hadn’t stuck with him right away, and thinking on it now, he could kick himself for not having called notice to it the moment he had seen it. It had been on the knife sheath of Roderick Stranger, Private Investigator. ** “The sonofabitch was in arm’s reach,” Julio grumbled a few hours later, as he and a team of crime scene techs observed what remained of Assan Biker. “He was right in front of me, and I let him go.” The M.E. and his assistant wordlessly motioned Julio to back away from the mutilated remains, rolling the body over. The assistant let out a groan as they did so, and quickly shuffled away after helping put the body bag under the victim. “What’s with Jerry? He’s not usually squeamish,” Julio observed to the M.E. “He likely just spotted what I did, detective,” the older man replied with a grimace. “Your victim’s severed, ah, ‘appendage’, is accounted for. It appears to have been shoved up his backside.” Julio sucked air through clenched teeth, shaking his head. The savagery that had gone into this latest attack had been swift, however, and much sloppier than the previous victims, likely as a result of the MAP Hunter (Julio hated himself for mentally accepting this label, but there it was) having felt the heat of the closing circle of law enforcement. The detective waved the M.E. off, then headed back through the luxury condo for Biker’s bedroom. Much to his surprise, none of the scene techs had been in the room yet, from all appearances. Julio cast a quick glance around the room, spotting an open laptop sitting on the bed. He made his way around with his latex gloves to retrieve it, halting as he spotted something resting on the dead man’s pillow- a small business card. For one Roderick Stranger, PI. On the back was written the following: “Come alone, detective.” Following this was an address, one he knew only vaguely from when he had first moved to the area of Amelia City. Between Amelia proper and North Perry, off the long, quiet country road that connected the city itself with its largest suburb, there was an old Iowa Highway Patrol station that had been out of service for a long time. He’d been out there twice since arriving in Amelia City, each time tracking rumors and street hubbub that resulted in the discovery of people who had gone missing and were presumed dead. Julio pocketed the card in his front pants pocket, closed the laptop, and brought it out into the living room, handing it over to a scene tech before excusing himself from the condo. ** Sometimes, when a person is confronted with the bizarre or the absurd, their brain performs a kind of trick in order to protect itself, shutting out entirely certain personal sensory input, then slowly allowing it to filter through to the conscious mind. Over the course of history, people who experience this phenomenon have frequently described the sensation as a kind of tingling or itching that creeps over their scalp. Detective Julio Ramos underwent this sensation as he idled his unmarked cruiser along the gravel pathway that led off the county road and through a wooded thicket toward the abandoned Highway Patrol station. The first of the oddities was the rapid onset of darkness, which only came to his tangible attention about fifty yards down the path when the vehicle’s sensor-activated headlights suddenly sprang alight to reveal the way ahead. At first, he thought nothing of it; after all, sunset was coming earlier and earlier as the season worked its way towards the first snowfalls in the region. But a quick glance over at the dashboard’s clock made this a curiosity that deserved a second glance, because according to that clock, it was only three in the afternoon. The second oddity landed gently in his ears as he pulled into the natural archway between the trees which opened up into a cracked but paved parking area in front of the decrepit old Highway Patrol station. His radio, which had previously been offering a quiet but audible string of Top 40 tunes, had at some point abruptly changed to a kind of discordant jumble of classical instrumentation, strings and brass and woodwinds all seeming to play a jangled mess of mismatched tunes. It’s like a 7th grade orchestra of kids all playing off of different sheet music books, he thought, pulling the cruiser into a faded spot fronting the concrete walkway up into the building proper. The third oddity, though it perhaps should not have surprised him, was the fact that the four tall arc sodium lamps flanking the front walkway of the station were working, dimly illuminating the area. As Julio clambered up out of his vehicle, he instinctively thumbed loose the clasp button on his holster, clearing his firearm free and flipping the safety off. “Not sure you’re going to need that, boy scout,” someone said nearby in a voice that sounded like it belonged at the original Woodstock music festival. Julio shifted toward the direction of the voice, the barrel of his weapon held steady toward the ground, per his training, and immediately he felt his mouth dry up and his throat clench in preparation of a scream. Standing just off to one side of the walkway on the grass, just visible in the span of the lamplight, was what appeared to be a cow, placidly chewing a mouthful of grass. But to call it simply a cow would be rather limited, given its unique qualities; its coat did not appear to be the traditional black and white, for one thing. No, this specimen, standing in profile to Julio, head turned to look directly at him as it chewed, appeared to have a coat colored in the various hues of the rainbow, in wide but equal-sized stripes. From its underside hung an udder sack that appeared to be covered in some kind of necrotic rot, oozing a kind of sickly green pus from pustules pocking its surface. The smell of the thing, a blend of decay and, for some reason, coffee, jarred Julio’s sense of reason almost as hard as the sight of it. And on its head, there stood two sets of eyes. The normal, bovine eyes just sort of looked at him with a half-lidded glare, while above them, a set of glowing, scarlet slashes glimmered balefully at him. The voice, the words, had come from the cow. “What the fuck,” Julio managed to croak. “I wouldn’t leave the man inside waiting too long,” the cow replied, its words carrying cleanly despite the fact that it still looked, for all intents and purposes, to be chewing its cud methodically. “He ain’t exactly the most patient guy I ever worked with.” Julio felt his gorge rising, and the urge to raise his weapon and pump multiple rounds into this bovine abomination nearly won the day. The only thing that kept his weapon down was the recognition that this, thing, was perhaps the most Amelia City thing he had ever come across. What would be the point of trying to shoot it, he mused. It’s like so much else in this godforsaken city; there, but not really there. Steeling himself, and with his weapon still in hand, Julio forced himself to look away from the Technicolor cow and march up the cracked walkway toward the station. The glass door fronting the station appeared to be covered in a layer of grime, obscuring his view inside until he pulled it open, revealing a front vestibule that had been turned into what looked like some kind of old-fashioned hunters’ lodge, complete with a working fireplace, a crackling fire warming the broad chamber opposite where Julio stood. Dominating the center of the room was what appeared to be a figure bound to an old wooden chair, largely covered under some kind of blanket. Seated just a few feet away, his long, wicked-looking blade resting on his leg, was the queer cowboy fellow himself, Roderick, his facial features no longer obscured in the light thrown from the fireplace and a nearby lamp. He was a ruggedly handsome sort, with the windburned, stubbly cheeks one might see on an Old Western gunfighter, which struck Julio as perfectly in keeping with the rest of his overall portrayal. “I was starting to wonder if you were gonna show up, detective,” Roderick intoned, not turning his head to look Julio’s way, but instead still keeping his face toward the unidentified figure struggling against his rope bonds in the chair nearby. “But Clancy tells me you came alone, which is good. He can’t give milk, but he’s a good lookout when one is required.” The odd man rose from his seat, and pointed with the tip of his blade toward a small, round table off to one side of the room, to Julio’s right, where there stood an open laptop computer. “You should have a look at that, detective Ramos. It’s interesting reading.” Roderick flapped his blade toward Julio as if to prompt him into approaching the computer. Training took over, and Julio, responding to the blade’s movement, fired two rounds into the man’s head. Roderick’s head snapped backward, but the rest of his body didn’t move so much as an inch. Slowly, cartoonishly slowly, Roderick brought his head back down, blood streaming down his face in a thin rivulet that turned into barely a trickle as a pair of crumpled bullets pushed back out of his head, dropping to the floor. Julio watched, his throat almost clenching shut, as the gunshot wound, widened from the back-to-back shots, suctioned closed, as if nothing had happened, and the blood on Roderick’s face faded away. The knife hand swept from its tip pointing at the computer, to now pointing at the detective. “Put the knife down,” Julio barked in response, raising his weapon and aiming square at the side of Roderick’s head. The cowboy fellow slowly turned his head to look at Julio, his weapon arm lowering to his side at the same time. “Drop it!” “Detective, I’m not in the habit of taking orders from much of anybody, except the bird,” the stranger said evenly, though with a slight hint of menace threaded through his tone, the corners of his mouth tugging down. “He runs the show around here, so I haven’t really got a choice in that; he made me what I am, and he can just as easily unmake me, I suspect. But you?” Roderick shook his head, and the frown quirked into a wry grin. “No, sir. Besides, I’m pretty sure you know exactly what would happen if you pulled that trigger on me again.” Julio slipped his index finger back inside the trigger guard, cold sweat beading on the back of his neck. Yes, he did indeed understand precisely what would happen if he once more shot the creature calling itself Roderick- a bullet wound would appear, but the thing would not be stopped, and faster than he could blink, Julio Ramos would find himself choking on his own blood with that blade buried in either his throat or his chest. He slid his finger out of the trigger guard, thumbed the safety back on, and holstered the weapon. “Wise choice,” Roderick rumbled, once more pointing toward the laptop with his knife. “Read.” Julio, his legs feeling like they might fold under him at any moment now, caught a whiff of the man now, a blend of tobacco, whiskey and sweat. He strode over to the table, and started scanning the screen. There appeared to be two windows open, side by side, and he moved the cursor over the left window, reading through what appeared to be several chat exchanges between someone dubbed ‘Blockerman’ and several other individuals. After a few exchanges, Julio realized that he recognized several of these usernames; they were victims of the MAP Hunter. The right-hand window appeared to be an online banking account, and it showed a series of funds transfers from third parties, all of them also victims in Julio’s case. Scrolling to the top of the page, Julio felt his stomach twist as he discovered who was receiving money from the pedophiles. He whipped his head to look over at Roderick, who now stood right next to his restrained victim, his left hand holding the covering blanket. With a single twist, the cowboy-like figure tossed the blanket aside, revealing a bucking, thrashing Commissioner with a sock gag stuffed in his mouth and a swollen, blackened left eye. “This man touched no innocent child himself, you see, detective,” said Roderick evenly. “But he did accept money to make sure that everybody under his command either looked in the wrong places, or went about handling ‘more important’ cases. He protected these depraved cretins, who knows for how long.” Julio shook his head slightly, unsure of himself. The evidence of what Roderick was saying was plain as day, right there on that laptop screen, but he had to wonder how much of this could be trusted as real, definitive proof. Given all of the absurdity he had witnessed since the start of this case, especially since arriving at this abandoned Highway Patrol station, how could he be sure? But this question was shunted aside in his mind almost immediately with another, much more reasonable one, a question he could actually ask out loud. “Why? What does any of this have to do with, you? With whatever you are,” he asked, forcing himself to sound more controlled than he felt. “I wasn’t lying about everything before, you know,” Roderick replied. “I really am something of a detective myself. I find people around this city, these towns, who are just up to no good, and I just sort of, even the scales, as it were,” he said, holding up his free hand and waggling it back and forth. “That’s the task that was given to me. It’s my duty, you see. You know about duty, detective Ramos, don’t you? Isn’t that why you became a law enforcement officer?” “This,” Julio said, shaking his head and sniffling, on the verge of losing his failing grasp on sanity. “This isn’t the same thing.” “You’re quite right,” said Roderick. “It’s a close cousin, though. And much as you might want to deny it, you know as well as I do that my way, Amelia’s way, is necessary sometimes. It’s brutal, but it’s just. Now, I understand full well that you may feel the need to protect this man, to save him from me,” said Roderick, now aiming his blade at the moaning Commissioner. “You may want to place him under arrest, and present that computer of his as evidence in a case to have him locked up and sent away for the rest of his corrupt little life. I can understand that,” Roderick said with a grave nod. “I can even respect it. If you feel that’s what you have to do, I will not stop you. But you have a choice to make right now, detective. Will this man face the justice of the system sworn to by detective Julio Ramos,” he asked, pointing the tip of the blade toward Julio. “Or will he face the one sworn to by the stranger named Roderick, He of the Blade,” he continued, pointing the tip at the underside of his own stubble-heavy chin. Julio looked to the computer, to the Commissioner, and then lastly, to the stranger named Roderick. He hung his head after a moment, then made several motions. He set his badge and his gun, still in its holster, on the round table, beside the laptop computer, and turned his back on the stranger and the Commissioner, letting out a long, heavy sigh. “Will they find the computer?” “I will make sure of it,” said Roderick behind him. “But they will not find your gun or your badge here, Julio. This I promise and swear in the name of Amelia. Now, go. Your duty here to the innocent is complete.” Julio strode away then, back out onto the station’s front walkway, back to the car. He would never again serve the people of Amelia; that, he determined, could be left to the queer mercies of the city’s otherworldly denizens. -Fin

Calkins-Treworgy #fiction #horror #WritingCommunity Part III- Decisions “Hell is empty, and all the devils are here.” -William Shakespeare “Well, shit,” Julio muttered to himself, hanging up on the attempted call. The number on the back of the private investigator’s card had gone to a dead end, an automated voice informing him that the number he was trying to dial was out of service. He followed this up by quickly hopping on the computer at his desk in the bullpen, and performing a quick search through the state of Iowa’s register for licensed private investigators. When no match for the name ‘Roderick Stranger’ came up, he felt a tightening in his gut, and thought, Oh, I fucked up. Immediately he sped down into the basement level of the station, bursting into Quinn’s fortress and startling the pale young computer tech enough to cause her to nearly fall back in her wheeled chair. Pinwheeling her arms, she barely maintained herself in an upright position, and she panted for a moment, glaring up at him. “Where’s the fire there, big guy,” she squeaked. “I need you to pull up and look through the last couple of hours of interior footage from the station, first and third floors, and the steps coming inside,” Julio said curtly. He handed her the P.I.’s card. “This guy came by, claiming he was looking into Biker on behalf of a private client, but the number’s disconnected, and his name doesn’t come up in the PI registration for the state. We have facial recognition software, though, right?” “Some of the newest and most expensive,” Quinn replied with a wry grin. “Let me take a look see here,” she said, wheeling herself over to a different workstation from the one she had been at when he burst in. The knife hand swept from its tip pointing at the computer, to now pointing at the detective. “Put the knife down,” Julio barked in response, raising his weapon and aiming square at the side of Roderick’s head. The cowboy fellow slowly turned his head to look at Julio, his weapon arm lowering to his side at the same time. “Drop it!” “Detective, I’m not in the habit of taking orders from much of anybody, except the bird,” the stranger said evenly, though with a slight hint of menace threaded through his tone, the corners of his mouth tugging down. “He runs the show around here, so I haven’t really got a choice in that; he made me what I am, and he can just as easily unmake me, I suspect. But you?” Roderick shook his head, and the frown quirked into a wry grin. “No, sir. Besides, I’m pretty sure you know exactly what would happen if you pulled that trigger on me again.” Julio slipped his index finger back inside the trigger guard, cold sweat beading on the back of his neck. Yes, he did indeed understand precisely what would happen if he once more shot the creature calling itself Roderick- a bullet wound would appear, but the thing would not be stopped, and faster than he could blink, Julio Ramos would find himself choking on his own blood with that blade buried in either his throat or his chest. He slid his finger out of the trigger guard, thumbed the safety back on, and holstered the weapon. “Wise choice,” Roderick rumbled, once more pointing toward the laptop with his knife. “Read.” Julio, his legs feeling like they might fold under him at any moment now, caught a whiff of the man now, a blend of tobacco, whiskey and sweat. He strode over to the table, and started scanning the screen. There appeared to be two windows open, side by side, and he moved the cursor over the left window, reading through what appeared to be several chat exchanges between someone dubbed ‘Blockerman’ and several other individuals. After a few exchanges, Julio realized that he recognized several of these usernames; they were victims of the MAP Hunter. The right-hand window appeared to be an online banking account, and it showed a series of funds transfers from third parties, all of them also victims in Julio’s case. Scrolling to the top of the page, Julio felt his stomach twist as he discovered who was receiving money from the pedophiles. He whipped his head to look over at Roderick, who now stood right next to his restrained victim, his left hand holding the covering blanket. With a single twist, the cowboy-like figure tossed the blanket aside, revealing a bucking, thrashing Commissioner with a sock gag stuffed in his mouth and a swollen, blackened left eye. “This man touched no innocent child himself, you see, detective,” said Roderick evenly. “But he did accept money to make sure that everybody under his command either looked in the wrong places, or went about handling ‘more important’ cases. He protected these depraved cretins, who knows for how long.” Julio shook his head slightly, unsure of himself. The evidence of what Roderick was saying was plain as day, right there on that laptop screen, but he had to wonder how much of this could be trusted as real, definitive proof. Given all of the absurdity he had witnessed since the start of this case, especially since arriving at this abandoned Highway Patrol station, how could he be sure? But this question was shunted aside in his mind almost immediately with another, much more reasonable one, a question he could actually ask out loud. “Why? What does any of this have to do with, you? With whatever you are,” he asked, forcing himself to sound more controlled than he felt. “I wasn’t lying about everything before, you know,” Roderick replied. “I really am something of a detective myself. I find people around this city, these towns, who are just up to no good, and I just sort of, even the scales, as it were,” he said, holding up his free hand and waggling it back and forth. “That’s the task that was given to me. It’s my duty, you see. You know about duty, detective Ramos, don’t you? Isn’t that why you became a law enforcement officer?” “This,” Julio said, shaking his head and sniffling, on the verge of losing his failing grasp on sanity. “This isn’t the same thing.” “You’re quite right,” said Roderick. “It’s a close cousin, though. And much as you might want to deny it, you know as well as I do that my way, Amelia’s way, is necessary sometimes. It’s brutal, but it’s just. Now, I understand full well that you may feel the need to protect this man, to save him from me,” said Roderick, now aiming his blade at the moaning Commissioner. “You may want to place him under arrest, and present that computer of his as evidence in a case to have him locked up and sent away for the rest of his corrupt little life. I can understand that,” Roderick said with a grave nod. “I can even respect it. If you feel that’s what you have to do, I will not stop you. But you have a choice to make right now, detective. Will this man face the justice of the system sworn to by detective Julio Ramos,” he asked, pointing the tip of the blade toward Julio. “Or will he face the one sworn to by the stranger named Roderick, He of the Blade,” he continued, pointing the tip at the underside of his own stubble-heavy chin. Julio looked to the computer, to the Commissioner, and then lastly, to the stranger named Roderick. He hung his head after a moment, then made several motions. He set his badge and his gun, still in its holster, on the round table, beside the laptop computer, and turned his back on the stranger and the Commissioner, letting out a long, heavy sigh. “Will they find the computer?” “I will make sure of it,” said Roderick behind him. “But they will not find your gun or your badge here, Julio. This I promise and swear in the name of Amelia. Now, go. Your duty here to the innocent is complete.” Julio strode away then, back out onto the station’s front walkway, back to the car. He would never again serve the people of Amelia; that, he determined, could be left to the queer mercies of the city’s otherworldly denizens. -Fin
